tier_reason: Independent third-party shootout (ahaoboy/js-engine-benchmark, v8-v7 suite run by scripts/update.ts from .github/workflows/update.yml) puts SpiderMonkey 147.0 at Score 19137 / 25455 / 19049 (ubuntu / macos-arm64 / windows) against QuickJS 1217 / 1761 / 1067 and Duktape 489 / 905 / 371; the code is public but the runners' CPU model and the engines' compiler flags are not stated, so it falls short of A.

corrections.claimed_speedup: v8-v7 Score (higher is better), ubuntu / macos-arm64 / windows: SpiderMonkey 147.0 19137 / 25455 / 19049 vs QuickJS 2026.06.04 1217 / 1761 / 1067 vs Duktape 489 / 905 / 371. About 15.7x QuickJS and 39x Duktape on ubuntu (derived from page data). Wall time for the whole suite on ubuntu: SpiderMonkey 20 s, QuickJS 37 s, Duktape 70 s. Score per MB of binary on ubuntu is lower than the small interpreters (468/M vs QuickJS 1190/M and Duktape 1352/M).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: SpiderMonkey is Mozilla's official prebuilt jsshell zip (archive.mozilla.org/pub/firefox/releases/<latest development version>/jsshell/), fetched by ahaoboy/spidermonkey-build download.sh, so it is Mozilla's release build; QuickJS and Duktape come from the suite owner's quickjs-build and duktape-build repos via the ahaoboy/js-engine-setup action (strip: true); compiler and flags for those builds are not stated on the benchmark page.
corrections.caveats: Engines are installed as prebuilt binaries through the suite owner's js-engine-setup action; the SpiderMonkey binary is Mozilla's official jsshell for the latest Firefox development release (the from-source job in ahaoboy/spidermonkey-build, whose meson.build carries the esr115 label, is disabled with if: false), so the exact revision behind 'version 147.0' was not pinned. CPU model of the GitHub Actions runners is not stated and each engine runs once per platform with no repetitions or variance, so this is short of tier A. The score is one v8-v7 aggregate (an older suite of eight benchmarks) and engines run as shells, so startup counts in the wall time. SpiderMonkey runs with its JIT while QuickJS and Duktape are interpreters, so this measures a different class of engine; binary size is 40.8 MB vs 1 MB (QuickJS) and 370 KB (Duktape) on ubuntu. The repo URL is the Firefox monorepo because SpiderMonkey source lives under js/src; embedding it is far heavier than QuickJS or Duktape.

notes: All README numbers (snapshot 10/5/2026, 4:04:34 AM) match the record; the record's 'built through spidermonkey-build/esr115' caveat was wrong: the active workflow job downloads Mozilla's official jsshell release zip. Shortcomings: JIT engine against interpreters, single run per engine on unnamed GitHub runner CPUs, 40.8 MB binary vs 1 MB QuickJS, heavy embedding cost.

tier_reason: Independent third-party shootout (r-lyeh scriptorium, public-domain harness bench.cc + run.bat + tests/fib.tvm and tests/fib.lua) lists TinyVM 0.786 s vs Lua 1.341 s on fib(34); compiler is named (VS2015 RC / VS2013) but flags are not and the CPU is given only as 'AMD A10 3.8 GHz', so it is short of A; same tier as the other scriptorium entries (Terra, Pawn, chibi-scheme).

corrections.workload: Recursive Fibonacci fib(34) (result 433494437). The scriptorium harness (bench.cc, driven by run.bat) runs each engine's standalone executable through system() ('tinyvm\tvm tests\fib.tvm', 'lua tests\fib.lua'), so each time is whole-process wall clock including startup and parsing, averaged over 5 runs; the README table keeps the lowest of the recorded averages per engine. The TinyVM row runs a hand-written assembly-like fib.tvm program (register accumulator, recursive call/ret).
corrections.caveats: Single micro-benchmark (recursive fib(34)) from July 2015 on a Windows 7 AMD A10 3.8 GHz with MSVC 2013/2015 and unstated flags; the page says 'take it with a grain of salt'. Engines are timed as separate executables (process start-up included), not embedded from C++ despite the suite's stated requirement. The Lua row is the LuaDist build (version and flags not stated); bench.csv holds two Lua averages, 2.359 s and 1.341 s, and the table keeps the faster one, while TinyVM's five averages span 0.786-0.815 s, so the 1.7x rests on Lua's better record. The comparison is hand-written VM assembly against interpreted Lua source, not a realistic scripting workload: TinyVM is an assembly-level VM with no high-level language. The TinyVM repo is not archived but its last commit is 2018-03-22 (abandoned); the benchmark repo r-lyeh-archived/scriptorium is archived. The TinyVM README makes no performance claims.

notes: Numbers match the scriptorium README and bench.csv (TinyVM 0.786 s, Lua 1.341 s, 'x01.7', rank 9 of 50); fib.tvm computes the right result, so the evidence is valid. Shortcomings: one 2015 micro-benchmark, process-level timing incl. startup, Lua's other recorded run was 2.36 s, assembly program against Lua source, abandoned since 2018. Record's 'repo is archived' and 'README could not be fetched' were wrong and are corrected in caveats.

tier_reason: First-party dashboard from the Escargot project's own self-hosted ARM64 runner; the harness (tools/monthly-engine-benchmark.py via .github/workflows/monthly-engine-benchmark.yml) and raw JSON are public and the CPU is identifiable from cpu_info (Arm part 0xd0c), but the compiler and version are not recorded, so it is not A, and first-party numbers with partial methodology stay at C.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: Escargot built by tools/monthly-engine-benchmark.py with CMake -DCMAKE_BUILD_TYPE=Release -DESCARGOT_DEPLOY=ON -DESCARGOT_THREADING=ON -DESCARGOT_TCO=ON -DESCARGOT_ENABLE_SHELL=ON (Ninja) into out/monthly-engine-release-arm64; QuickJS 2026-06-04 built from the official tarball with its own Makefile ('make qjs', upstream default -O2) and run as 'qjs --std --stack-size 8388608'; compiler and version not recorded; glibc 2.39 runtime for all engines.
corrections.hardware: aarch64 Linux 6.8.0-1063-aws, 16 cores, Arm CPU implementer 0x41 part 0xd0c (Neoverse N1 class, an AWS Graviton2-type host, inferred from the CPU part id and kernel), engine pinned to one core with taskset and the memory monitor on another
corrections.caveats: First-party dashboard published by the Escargot project from its own CI runner; the harness and raw JSON are public but the compiler is not recorded, so capped at tier C. QuickJS uses less memory than Escargot on SunSpider (5.3 vs 14.2 MiB average RSS), so the memory advantage only holds on the larger Octane and Web Tooling workloads. The score gains over QuickJS are 20-30%, not an order of magnitude. On the same dashboard V8 d8 --jitless (also no JIT) is faster than Escargot on all three suites (SunSpider 694.6 ms, Octane 2300, Web Tooling 2.02 runs/s), though it uses more memory (Octane 152.8 MiB, Web Tooling 265.8 MiB average RSS); full d8 with JIT is roughly 11x Escargot on Octane. A prebuilt ARM32 dashboard exists too but was not opened. The pretty dashboard on samsung.github.io was not reachable; numbers were read from the gh-pages branch file latest.json.

notes: All speed and fixed-work memory numbers in the record match latest.json (measured 2026-10-04, Escargot fc608b59b); harness and build options are public in tools/monthly-engine-benchmark.py. Shortcomings: first-party CI dashboard, compiler not recorded, only 1.2-1.3x over QuickJS, loses to V8 --jitless on speed, uses more memory than QuickJS on SunSpider.
